Our key insight is that a concrete execution trace provides not only behavioral evidence for recovering exploit logic, but also runtime semantics that enable precise code synthesis and verification. We design TracExp, a trace-driven framework that combines a dual decompiler, which fuses symbolic lifting with concrete runtime values to produce semantically enriched pseudocode, and a sketch-based synthesis and refinement mechanism that grounds LLM generation in execution context and ensures semantic correctness. Evaluated on 321 real-world DeFi attacks collected over 20 months, TracExp achieves 94.70% generation, 83.80% compilable, and 57.01% verifiable rates, at an average cost of ∼$0.1 per case. Moreover, we contributed 33 previously unavailable PoCs within 2 days to DeFiHackLabs, and all were accepted and merged, earning $900 in bounties, demonstrating both the practical effectiveness and real-world impact.
authors: Xing Su; Hao Wu; Hanzhong Liang; Yunlin Jiang; Yuxi Cheng; Yating Liu; Fengyuan Xu; Sheng Zhong
venue: IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE)

title: SecChain: Operationalizing Security Guidelines for Multi-agent Smart Contract Generation
abstract: Smart contracts generated by large language models (LLMs) can compile yet still violate basic security obligations, and existing generation frameworks largely treat security as post-hoc verification rather than as a constraint that persists throughout generation and repair. We present SecChain, a multi-agent smart-contract generation framework built around a persistent SecuritySpec artifact that makes requirement-level security obligations explicit and preserves them across planning, coding, testing, auditing, and fixing. Five LLM-powered agents collaborate with a fully deterministic Coordinator through stage-specific procedures, deterministic pre-test verification, and nested repair loops, while an Auditor provides complementary semantic review grounded in a three-layer security knowledge base. We evaluate SecChain on 1,000 contracts from the finite-state-machine-guided smart-contract generation (FSM-SCG) dataset against vanilla GPT-4o, GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and the FSM-SCG framework. SecChain achieves an 89.0% final compilation rate and a Zero Risk Contract Proportion (ZRCP) of 60.3%, compared with 12.7% for vanilla GPT-4o and 23.3% for FSM-SCG. With a GPT-4o backbone, SecChain still outperforms the tested vanilla current-generation models (GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6) on the primary security metrics.
authors: Dianxiang Sun; Liming Nie; Yang Liu
venue: IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE)

title: Learning from Failures: A Failure-Driven Prompt Refinement for LLM-Based Vulnerability Analysis
abstract: Large Language Models have emerged as promising tools for software vulnerability analysis, but their effectiveness depends heavily on prompt design. Existing research primarily compares prompting strategies using aggregate performance metrics, providing limited insight into why models fail or how prompts can be improved systematically. We propose Failure-Driven Prompt Refinement (FDPR), a methodology that analyzes recurring model failures to guide evidence-based prompt refinement. Using the Damn Vulnerable Java Application (DVJA), we identify recurring failure modes, including false positives, false negatives, unsupported reasoning, and CWE misclassification, and translate them into targeted prompt refinements. We then evaluate the resulting prompt on the Juliet Test Suite and perform cross-model validation to assess generalizability. The results show that failure-driven refinement improves the reliability of LLM-based vulnerability analysis while yielding reusable prompt design principles. More broadly, this work demonstrates that recurring model failures provide a principled foundation for prompt engineering, enabling the systematic development of more reliable LLM-based vulnerability analysis systems.
authors: Mandana Ghadamian; David Mohaisen

title: Case-Level Verification in Scanner-LLM Cascades: Overcoming the Alert Aggregation Bottleneck to Expand the FRR-TPR Trade-off Space
abstract: Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST) scanners achieve high recall but also produce a large number of false positives, resulting in substantial manual triage costs. Large Language Models (LLMs), when used for independent detection, achieve extremely high recall (95.4%-100%) but also exhibit prohibitively high false positive rates (49.6%-85.0%), precluding their use as standalone replacements for scanners. A natural solution is a two-stage cascade consisting of scanner detection followed by LLM verification. However, a verification-granularity issue that has long been overlooked in practice creates a structural bottleneck: alert aggregation binds multiple true and false cases into a shared decision unit, such that removing a false positive inevitably eliminates true positives aggregated within the same alert group. This creates a trade-off bottleneck between the False-positive Reduction Rate (FRR) and the True-positive Rate (TPR). We formalize this bottleneck by showing that the alert-level false-positive set is a subset of the case-level false-positive set, and introduce a Case-Level, per-case verification strategy that shifts the decision granularity from the alert level to the instance level, independently replaying HTTP requests and making an independent determination for each detected case. Evaluation on the dual testbeds of Damn Vulnerable Web Application (DVWA) and WebGoat shows that the empirically best Alert-Level operating point achieves FRR=42.86% (TPR=51.7%). The Case-Level Baseline achieves FRR=47.6%, an improvement of 4.7 percentage points (+4.7 pp), while the Case-Focused Evidence Verification Prompt (CEV-Prompt) increases TPR from 55.2% to 62.1% at the same FRR.
authors: Hao Sun; Yibin Yao; Chaohai Xie; Yuqun Lin

title: A Survey on LLM-Integrated Hardware Design Verification
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being integrated into hardware verification to automate specification interpretation, verification-artifact generation, debugging, formal reasoning, and tool orchestration. This survey provides a systematic review of LLM-assisted hardware functional verification across SystemVerilog assertion generation, stimulus and testbench generation, bug localization and design repair, model checking and equivalence checking, SAT/SMT optimization, and emerging agentic verification workflows. We organize the literature by methodology, verification objective, tool interaction, benchmark, and evaluation criterion, and examine both inference-time techniques--including prompting, retrieval, structured reasoning, and agentic workflows--and training-time adaptation. Across these areas, a common pattern emerges: LLMs are most effective as semantic reasoning, search, and orchestration components embedded within verification-aware workflows, while simulators, formal engines, coverage tools, and solvers provide executable feedback and correctness evidence. However, tool acceptance alone does not establish verification correctness, since assertions, tests, repairs, or proofs may satisfy available checks without faithfully capturing the complete design intent. We therefore identify semantic alignment between specifications and verification evidence, scalable integration with deterministic tools, generalization to unseen designs, and rigorous evaluation of correctness, cost, robustness, and human effort as key challenges. Finally, we discuss emerging directions toward specification-centered, neuro-symbolic, and persistent agentic verification systems that combine LLM flexibility with independently checkable verification evidence.
authors: Hao Zheng; Jaime Rafael Imperial; Bardia Nadimi; Xiangfei Kong

title: Multimodal generative cyber forensics network for unified malware intelligence synthesis through temporal evidence alignment, neuro-symbolic hypergraph reasoning, and cognitive threat attributions
abstract: Abstract Cyber-forensic investigations increasingly involve heterogeneous evidence, including phishing audio, malicious text and scripts, executable binaries, memory artifacts, and network traffic. Existing approaches generally analyze these sources independently or perform sample-level fusion without explicitly addressing temporal asynchrony, higher-order forensic relationships, missing attack stages, counterfactual threat evolution, and attribution uncertainty. This paper presents a Multimodal Generative Cyber Forensics Network comprising CTEEN for temporal-semantic alignment, NSFRH for higher-order forensic reasoning, GASRE for evidence-constrained attack-stage reconstruction, CMES for counterfactual malware-evolution analysis, and CTAECO for confidence-aware candidate-category attribution. The evaluation used VirusShare, CIC-MalMem-2022, the Android Malware Corpus, the Malware Traffic Repository, and an Integrated Controlled Multimodal Benchmark constructed from source pools containing approximately 52,000 malware records, 1.8 million network-flow records, 24,000 textual or script artifacts, and 12,500 phishing or social-engineering audio recordings. Comparisons were conducted against Cyber Code Intelligence, AI-Based Malware Analysis, Multimodal Pre-trained Fusion, and LLM-MalDetect using identical eligible evidence groups, preprocessing outputs, partitions, and metric definitions. Across 25 matched partition–seed observations, the proposed framework achieved 99.26 ± 0.18% classification accuracy (95% CI: 99.19–99.33%), 99.20 ± 0.21% F1-score, and 99.66 ± 0.12% AUC. It further obtained 98.46% mean controlled alignment accuracy, 98.68% evidence-constrained reconstruction accuracy, 99.04% benchmark-defined candidate-category attribution accuracy, and 99.0% overall forensic-intelligence reliability. Accuracy decreased to 95.18% under temporally disjoint testing and 92.34% under family-disjoint testing. Leakage audits, negative controls, matched statistical tests, and alternative-design ablations further supported the findings. The complete framework contained 96.3 million trainable parameters and required 12.8 GB of peak memory, with a mean inference latency of 73.2 ms per complete multimodal episode (13.7 episodes/s) under the reported computational environment. These requirements indicate that deployment on resource-constrained platforms would require model compression or inference optimization. Reviewer 3, Comment 3) The results demonstrate effective evidence-constrained multimodal reasoning under the controlled benchmark but do not establish natural incident-level correspondence, definitive real-world attribution, or universal forensic performance.
authors: Rijvan Beg; Rajesh Kumar Pateriya; Deepak Singh Tomar; Ghanshyam Raghuwanshi; Surendra Solanki

title: Correct Verdicts, Flawed Reasoning: Structured Auditing of LLM-based Vulnerability Reasoning
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for automated software vulnerability analysis. Binary classification alone is insufficient; practitioners need explanations to triage bugs and engineer patches. Standard practice relies on Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, but free-form reasoning allows models to obscure logical leaps, hallucinated execution steps, and internal inconsistencies behind plausible prose. Our manual audit reveals that approximately 60% of correct vulnerability verdicts are accompanied by fabricated or unverifiable claims, and free-form explanations allow reasoning errors to evade LLM-as-a-judge evaluation. We present Vulnerability Explanation Reasoning Auditor (VERA), an automated framework for auditing LLM vulnerability reasoning. Rather than accepting free-form text, VERA asks models to output a Structured Reasoning Record (SRR) encoding tracked pointers, memory operations, and state transitions in machine-readable fields. A multi-stage judge audits each SRR against eight reasoning failure modes using deterministic checks, with LLM calls reserved for semantic interpretation. The standardized SRR schema also enables automated mutation testing to benchmark judges at scale without human annotation. Our evaluation shows reasoning flaws occur in correct verdicts just as frequently as incorrect ones, and VERA exposes 87% of reasoning errors that free-form LLM-as-judge systematically miss.
authors: Boyue Caroline Hu; Kaivalya Ahir; Ronghao Ni; Limin Jia

title: Where Did the Repair First Go Wrong? Localizing the Origins of Silent Failures in Agentic Vulnerability Repair
abstract: Localizing where an LLM-based agent first fails to uphold security during a repair can show which stage of its workflow needs an additional safeguard. This is difficult for silent failures, which are patches that pass syntactic and functional checks but still contain a security vulnerability. Because such patches give no observable failure signal, existing failure attribution methods, which rely on observed task failures and labelled failure steps, are less suited to them. We propose Security Awareness Gap Evaluation (SAGE), a trace-based method that combines an assessment of the security reasoning recorded at each turn with the reconstructed code history to identify the earliest turn at which a repair diverges from the task's security intent. We evaluate SAGE on 95 confirmed silent failures drawn from 3,684 repair traces produced by six agent frameworks and six base models on SecurityEval and CVEfixes. SAGE assigned an origin in 93 cases. Most origins were an unaddressed security requirement or an inadequate defence choice, and only five coincided with the code change itself. When the agent introduced the vulnerable code, the origin preceded the write in 14 of 19 cases. Repeated scoring and a second judge reproduced the origin type more consistently than the exact turn, and agreement was lowest for traces that kept only the final file.
authors: Wenji Bai; Muhammad Waseem; Zeeshan Rasheed; Jaakko Peltonen; Pekka Abrahamsson

title: Evidence-Grounded Logic Vulnerability Detection for Smart Contracts via Runtime Context Reasoning
abstract: Smart contracts are foundational to DeFi, yet detecting business-logic vulnerabilities, i.e., execution is syntactically correct but violates a contract’s intended behavior, remains difficult. Most recent LLM-based approaches still follow a largely static, source-code–centric auditing paradigm. In practice, however, smart contracts are inherently stateful: many logic flaws emerge only under specific contract states and across particular state transitions. As a result, code-only auditing can produce false positives and miss true vulnerabilities. To address this gap, we present RcAudit, a system for detecting smart-contract logic vulnerabilities via runtime-context–enhanced LLM reasoning. RcAudit constructs a Contract Logic Knowledge Base that captures contract behavior from multiple perspectives to support LLM analysis. It then applies a state- and intent-aware fuzzing strategy to generate logic-critical runtime contexts, and performs LLM reasoning over selected contexts that exhibit potential intent–behavior inconsistencies to pinpoint vulnerabilities. We evaluate RcAudit on three real-world datasets. RcAudit identifies 74 of 132 known logic vulnerabilities with high precision (96.9%), achieving 117.6% higher detection than the strongest baseline. Importantly, RcAudit further uncovers 22 zero-day vulnerabilities in real-world projects.
authors: Guan-Zhong Gong; Yu-Cong Jiang; Rong Jian; Xiao-Tao Feng; Zhi-Han Wei; Qi Li; Ke Xu
venue: Proceedings of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering

title: From Circuits to Policies: A Review and Taxonomy of Decision Making and Strategy Selection in LLMs and LLM Agents
abstract: Large language models and the agents built on them can reach the same outcome through different internal computations, reasoning trajectories, and system-level policies. Existing reviews typically treat mechanistic interpretability, reasoning, agent architectures, and safety separately, leaving no common framework for analyzing how a system represents alternatives, evaluates them, commits to one, executes it, and revises that choice. This article presents a structured review and a faceted taxonomy of decision making and strategy selection in LLMs and LLM-based agents. The framework separates system locus—model, harness, or their tested interaction—from temporal scope—a single forward pass or call, a reasoning episode, or an agent trajectory—and decomposes decision making into six functional stages from state representation to update or termination. Five claim-specific evidential relations distinguish behavioral observation, representation decoding, causal influence, controlled manipulation, and mechanistic explanation, while robustness is assessed separately across prompts, tasks, models, harness configurations, and independent replication. Across the literature, evidence is strongest for local mechanisms within individual model calls and substantially weaker for persistent strategies across agent trajectories. The central unresolved gap is cross-scope continuity: few studies follow the same decision variable from internal representation through commitment, executed action, and subsequent feedback. A July 2026 agent-security incident is used to illustrate how the framework converts observed coordination and constraint circumvention into testable causal hypotheses.
authors: Christina Stodt

title: What Current AI Benchmarks Leave Unmeasured: Modality, Search, Citations, and Implications (for Safety Evaluations)
abstract: Large language model (LLM) benchmark evaluations are routinely used to support claims about model safety, reliability, and deployment readiness. Yet most evaluations rely on a single access modality (model APIs), perform a single run per prompt, and report accuracy as the primary outcome metric, without accounting for conditions such as web search that may have effects on model behavior in deployment. We audit these assumptions for one of the most widely-used LLMs, comparing two modalities, ChatGPT's chat UI and OpenAI's API, with and without web search enabled. We use a stratified total sample of 401 prompts from two popular benchmarks, BBQ and SafetyBench, collecting 4,812 total responses across three repeated runs per prompt. Beyond standard performance measures, we evaluate model output dimensions including response consistency, response text similarity, citation grounding, and abstention behavior. For instance, chat UI responses were less accurate than API responses on both benchmarks with search disabled. Enabling web search reduced accuracy by up to 8 percentage points, and even reversed the direction of modality performance trends for one benchmark. Repeated runs of the same prompt produced inconsistent responses in up to 21% of prompts. The two modalities also grounded answers in different citations, and abstention behavior was also inconsistent across both modalities. These results suggest that the simple accuracy numbers reported in most benchmarking can obscure important forms of model behavioral variation relevant to AI safety assessments. We argue that AI safety evaluations should systematically account for modality, multi-run consistency, search conditions, and response-level behaviors to better reflect how deployed AI systems behave in practice.
authors: Ro Encarnación; Tina Behzad; Emma Lurie; Danaë Metaxa
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI Ethics and Society

title: Unanimously Wrong: Certified Abstention from How Medical LLM Consensus Forms
abstract: In clinical practice, agreement among independent experts is treated as evidence of reliability, and multi-round consensus has become a core mechanism of agentic medical question-answering systems. When such a system must decide whether to trust its own answer, the prevailing signal is again agreement, now among the sampled answers. But agreement is a fragile proxy for correctness. A system can be unanimously wrong, returning the same incorrect answer on every sample, and on these questions agreement-based signals carry no information. The cause is that these signals read only the final state of the consensus and discard how it was reached. Agreement that was reached by resolving disagreement with evidence looks identical, at the end, to agreement that was present from the first sample because every sample shares one misconception. ProbeGuard is a certified abstention framework that bases the abstention decision on how the consensus formed. Process features trace agreement trajectories, minority persistence, and retrieval saturation. For unanimous votes, rationale semantic entropy checks whether the reasons behind the vote cohere, and an active probe retrieves counter-evidence and measures whether the consensus survives. A stratified Learn-then-Test calibration then converts these scores into a distribution-free bound on selective risk. We evaluate ProbeGuard on three medical QA benchmarks and a hard-frontier reference, with a published multi-round agentic RAG substrate, against six abstention baselines. On MedQA, 13.4% of unanimous votes are wrong, and no agreement-based signal can flag them. Process signals raise the discrimination of correct from incorrect consensus from chance to 0.696 AUROC. The certified rule answers six in ten unanimous-layer questions at an observed selective risk of 9.0%, and nine in ten once in-domain calibration data accumulate.
authors: Xiaoyang Wang; Tianrui Wang; Christopher C. Yang

title: EyeSeek: a large language model for screening and improving health literacy in primary eye care
abstract: Resource constraints and low health literacy hinder the effectiveness of primary eye care screening. Here, we developed EyeSeek, a specialized large language model (LLM) to provide residents with personalized screening interpretations and guidance. We introduced a novel abstention-driven iterative learning framework to enhance reliability by detecting uncertainty, alongside a role-playing strategy for tailored communication. Findings demonstrated that our method can abstain and seek external answers when handling queries beyond its knowledge boundary, which reduces hallucination. In expert evaluation, EyeSeek outperformed several LLMs and primary care physicians in multiple dimensions. Readability analysis confirmed that EyeSeek adapted responses to Grade 3 ~ 8 levels, enabling more accessible communication for residents with varying educational backgrounds. Furthermore, we performed a single-center real-world prospective study comparing referral adherence between the EyeSeek-assisted group ( n = 84) and the unassisted group ( n = 86). The EyeSeek-assisted group demonstrated higher referral adherence ( P = 0.037) and improved health literacy compared with the unassisted group, with high user satisfaction. Given its multifaceted performance, EyeSeek holds promise as an adaptable digital solution to support primary eye care in community settings.
authors: Jieru Liu; Juzhao Zhang; Lianqiang Gan; Yi Xu; Tao Yu; Yajun Peng; Lina Lu; Jingkuan Song; Senlin Lin; Haidong Zou

title: Trustworthy large language models (LLMs) for power-system operations: From “Grid Copilots” to verifiable decision support
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed as “grid copilots” for alarm interpretation, procedural retrieval, incident summarization, scenario analysis, and tool-mediated power-system studies. This review combines a PRISMA 2020-informed systematic identification/screening component with structured qualitative synthesis across power systems, LLM agents, trustworthy AI, and safety-critical decision support. The documented review pathway identified 312 records, removed 48 duplicates, screened 264 records, and assessed 213 full-text articles; after incorporation of additional recent and methodological literature, the current manuscript draws on a total evidence base of 199 references. The synthesis shows that recent tool-using agents can execute power-flow/OPF and contingency workflows, but operational trust remains conditional on authenticated state/topology, valid models and constraints, solver/tool correctness, uncertainty calibration, deadline compliance, human authority, cybersecurity, and reconstructable audit evidence. We therefore present VDS-LLM-Grid as an evidence-informed conceptual reference architecture—not a validated deployment—that integrates six assurance layers: input/state grounding, constraint-aware reasoning, independent verification, calibrated uncertainty with abstention, human oversight, and governance/auditability within a cross-cutting cybersecurity boundary. The paper defines conditional “verifiable decision support,” mathematical system-level metrics, deadline-aware routing, and a study-level evidence map that prioritizes empirical end-to-end validation, constraint verification, calibration, latency, cybersecurity, robustness, and operator evaluation.
authors: Mohamad Fani Sulaima; Arora Jyotsna; Lukáš Herout; Ignacio Perez Gálvez; Ondřej Krejcar; Hamidreza Namazi

title: Ethical and governance challenges of large language models in power and energy systems: a review and framework for responsible AI deployment
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for forecasting, monitoring, diagnostics, predictive maintenance, and decision support in power and energy systems, yet their deployment in safety-critical infrastructures raises concerns regarding hallucination, bias, explainability, cybersecurity, accountability, and human oversight. This structured scoping and critical review synthesizes a 126-source evidence corpus and compares emerging LLM paradigms, including domain-adapted models, retrieval-augmented generation, multimodal and reasoning models, agentic systems, and MCP-enabled architectures. Particular attention is given to power-system-specific requirements such as SCADA/EMS/DMS integration, topology awareness, state estimation, power-flow and voltage constraints, N-1 security, protection coordination, and operator authority. Quantitative publication trends and comparative evidence analysis are used to identify methodological and deployment gaps in the literature. Building on these findings, a multi-layer governance framework is proposed that integrates data and model governance, deterministic engineering verification, cybersecurity safeguards, human authorization, auditability, and regulatory oversight. A distribution-network fault-diagnosis and service-restoration workflow, together with a staged validation protocol, illustrates practical implementation. The review concludes with measurable research priorities for trustworthy LLM-enabled energy systems.
authors: Mohamad Fani Sulaima; Sunny Arora; Ondřej Krejcar; Lukáš Herout; Hamidreza Namazi

title: Cloud‐Native and Distributed Systems for Efficient and Scalable Large Language Models—A Research Agenda
abstract: ABSTRACT Objective Large Language Models (LLMs) are rapidly transforming artificial intelligence applications, but their unprecedented computational, memory, communication, and data‐management demands pose significant challenges to existing computing infrastructures. Traditional cloud and distributed systems were not designed for the scale, dynamic execution patterns, heterogeneous hardware requirements, and service‐level demands of modern LLM workloads. This paper aims to examine how cloud‐native and distributed systems can evolve to support efficient, scalable, reliable, and sustainable LLM training and inference. Methods We conduct a structured analysis of representative research advances and practical developments in distributed LLM training, inference serving, cloud‐native orchestration, resource management, heterogeneous computing, and edge‐cloud intelligence. We organize the analysis around major system challenges, including computation, distributed execution and system software, resource management and serving, security and privacy, data management, and standardization. We further examine representative resource‐management strategies and emerging paradigms, including serverless inference, federated and decentralized learning, trustworthy distributed AI, and heterogeneous computing with emerging accelerators. Results Our analysis reveals that supporting LLMs at scale requires a transition from general‐purpose cloud infrastructure toward LLM‐aware, cross‐layer, and adaptive systems. Existing approaches have improved distributed execution, elastic resource management, multi‐tenant serving, and hardware utilization, but important gaps remain in cross‐layer coordination, workload‐aware orchestration, data and context management, interoperability, security, and system‐level optimization. Based on these gaps, we develop a research agenda covering future directions in sparse and heterogeneous computation, LLM‐enhanced system software, prompt and context management, autonomous cloud management, decentralized intelligence, edge‐cloud collaboration, personalized LLM services, and emerging computing paradigms. Conclusion Cloud‐native and distributed systems will play a central role in enabling the next generation of LLM services. Future infrastructures should evolve toward more intelligent, elastic, interoperable, secure, and heterogeneous platforms that jointly optimize computation, memory, communication, data, and service objectives. Continued advances in system design, standardization, and cross‐disciplinary collaboration will be essential for realizing scalable and sustainable LLM infrastructures.
authors: Minxian Xu; Jingfeng Wu; Shengye Song; Satish Narayana Srirama; Bahman Javad; Rajiv Ranjan; Devki Nandan Jha; Sa Wang; Wenhong Tian; Huanle Xu; Li Li; Zizhao Mo; Shuo Ren; Thomas Kunz; Petar Kochovski; Vlado Stankovski; Kejiang Ye; Chengzhong Xu; Rajkumar Buyya

title: Operationalizing OWASP LLM Top 10 Controls in Enterprise AI Platforms
abstract: Enterprises have moved large language model applications from pilot projects into production systems handling customer conversations, internal knowledge retrieval, and increasingly autonomous agentic workflows, introducing a risk surface that differs materially from what conventional application security programs address. OWASP has responded with the Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications, most recently revised in its 2025 edition, and a newly published Top 10 for Agentic Applications covering autonomous, tool-using systems. These taxonomies name and prioritize risk but leave engineering teams to translate categories such as prompt injection or excessive agency into controls that fit an existing cloud-native delivery pipeline. This paper proposes a reference architecture and implementation framework mapping each of the ten OWASP LLM Top 10 2025 categories to specific, deployable controls built on commonly used cloud primitives: managed model gateways, service mesh identity, retrieval-augmented generation pipelines, and continuous delivery tooling. The framework is informed by production engineering practice with retrieval-augmented generation and agentic workloads on Kubernetes using a managed foundation model service. Five real, publicly documented incidents, including a corporate data leak, a manipulated dealership chatbot, a legal ruling on chatbot liability, an indirect prompt injection exfiltration attack, and a zero-click vulnerability in a widely used enterprise copilot, are analyzed against the proposed controls to show where the framework would have reduced impact or prevented the incident outright. A four-stage maturity model helps organizations sequence adoption. Open challenges discussed include the immaturity of evaluation tooling for non-deterministic systems and the persistent tension between guardrail thoroughness and production latency.
authors: Sai Kumar Pola; Pavan Kumar Koneru

title: WebMCP: A Browser-Native navigator.modelContext Standard for Agentic Web Automation
abstract: Purpose: This paper examines WebMCP, a proposed browser-native web platform standard that lets websites expose explicit, schema-described tools to large language model agents, as an alternative to actuation, in which an agent simulates the clicks, keystrokes, and navigation a human would perform. Methodology: The paper analyzes WebMCP, incubated within the World Wide Web Consortium's Web Machine Learning Community Group and implemented as an origin trial in the Chrome browser beginning with Chrome 149. We describe WebMCP's architecture, including the browser-mediated JavaScript interface navigator.modelContext and a declarative HTML annotation form, and its relationship to Anthropic's Model Context Protocol; analyze its security and permission model; place it within a comparative design-space taxonomy alongside DOM automation, computer-use agents, and server-side Model Context Protocol integrations; and examine the emerging standardization landscape, including browser vendor positions and adjacent efforts such as the Agentic Commerce Protocol. A generalized use case illustrates how a composite retail website might expose search, filtering, and checkout tools under this model. All sources and data referenced in this manuscript are dated on or before June 30, 2026. Findings: WebMCP allows a website to register tools that an agent invokes directly rather than inferring actions from pixels or DOM structure, with a security model built on origin isolation, a dedicated Permissions Policy directive, and a human-in-the-loop confirmation mechanism for consequential actions. Open problems remain in cross-site tool discovery, adversarial tool poisoning, and the evaluation of agent-web interaction quality. Unique Contribution to Theory, Policy and Practice: For theory, the paper contributes a comparative design-space taxonomy that positions browser-native, declarative agent integration against actuation-based and server-side approaches. For practice, it gives web developers and agent builders a technical account of WebMCP's registration mechanisms, security model, and interaction flow. For policy, it informs browser vendors and standards bodies through its analysis of the standardization landscape and a research agenda for browser-native agent integration standards as this area continues to develop.
authors: Harsha Nooka; Suhas Madupuri

title: AdvRoNIDS: A Constraint-Aware Framework for Adversarially Robust Network Intrusion Detection via Min-Max Training and Attribution Analysis
abstract: Machine learning-based Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS) have become critical security infrastructure, but the vast majority of published research reports accuracy only on clean, unperturbed traffic, leaving their robustness to adversarial evasion unexplored. Existing research into adversarial robustness, when it has occurred, has largely imported image-domain approaches of unconstrained perturbation to network traffic, producing "adversarial" examples that could not possibly occur on a real network, and so failing to probe the true robustness of the system to real-world adversaries. We propose AdvRoNIDS, a constraint-aware adversarial robustness framework for NIDS that (i) trains a deep 1D-CNN classifier on flow-based features from the CICIDS2017 benchmark, (ii) crafts adversarial examples using the Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) and Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) restricted to a feasibility-constrained perturbation set (ПЅ) respecting feature immutability, non-negativity of cumulative counters, and empirical feature bounds, (iii) hardens the classifier through min-max adversarial training against this constrained attacker, and (iv) evaluates the resulting system using a transparent two-number benchmark of clean accuracy and accuracy-under-attack across a full perturbation-budget sweep. The undefended classifier collapses from 90.45% clean accuracy to 25.11% under realistic constrained attack at ε = 0.10, while the adversarially trained classifier retains 87.96% accuracy under the same attack, a 62.85 percentage-point improvement, with negligible cost to clean accuracy (90.45% to 90.86%). A SHAP-based attribution-drift analysis further demonstrates that this robustness arises mechanistically rather than incidentally: the undefended model's decision attribution shifts drastically under attack (mean drift 1.898), while the robust model's attribution remains substantially more stable (mean drift 0.923), a 51.4% reduction that is statistically significant (Mann-Whitney p<1.87×10−161,Cliff's δ = 0.70, a large effect). We additionally present an applied explainability and LLM-assisted incident-triage layer that translates the system's outputs into analyst-readable incident narratives. This work explicitly scopes itself to constrained feature-space robustness, leaving end-to-end packet-level attack realizability for future work.
authors: Akash Kushwaha; Abuzar A Dr. Mohammed
venue: Indian Journal of Computer Science and Technology

title: Trustworthy Phishing URL Detection Using Machine Learning: Performance Analysis and Future Directions
abstract: Over the years, Uniform Resource Locator (URL) Phishing has been a threat to online security because their scams exploit trust in a misleading URL to trick unsuspecting users into disclosing their username or passwords and other personal information. Not only that, but it is also crucial to identify these malicious URLs and ensure online platforms and users are protected. The ISCXURL2016 data was utilized for the purpose of analyzing the performance of different Machine Learning (ML) models in differentiating phishing and legitimate URLs in this paper. A wide range of classifiers were explored including the classic classifiers as well as more advanced ensemble classifiers. The results of the experiments indicate that ensemble-based boosting models can be more beneficial for URL phishing detection. HistGradientBoost achieved the highest accuracy of 98.47%, followed closely by LightGBM and XGBoost that both outperformed the accuracy of 98%. The other classifiers, RandomForest and ExtraTrees, also performed well with accuracy above 97% and traditional classifiers such as Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA) showed the poorest performance with an accuracy of 67.75%. The results show that the boosting-based ensembles provide a suitable negation of the complex and non-linear structure of phishing URLs. Along with empirical evaluation, it offers a Properties & Positioning viewpoint as well as the importance of the ML-based phishing detection in the broader context of cybersecurity issues. Moreover, it discusses the future directions, with Federated Learning (FL) in the context of decentralized and privacy-preserving collaboration and Large Language Models (LLM) in the context of semantic reasoning and flexibility. These insights together will provide the building blocks for more intelligent, adaptive and trustworthy phishing organizations.
authors: Omer ِAlmomani; Ahmad Shalaldeh; Mohammed Almaayah; Ahmad Saleh Shatat; Mohammed Madi; Mutasem K. Alsmadi; Ibrahim Mohammed Dweib
venue: International Journal of Advances in Soft Computing and its Applications

title: From Manual to LLM-Assisted Formal Verification of a PKCS#1 Signature Parser
abstract: Abstract Software engineering approaches assisted by Artificial Intelligence (AI) are receiving increasing attention. This work evaluates the ability of large language models (LLMs) to assist engineers in the formal verification process. We conduct an experiment using on a PKCS#1 (Public-Key Cryptography Standard) v1.5 signature parser that was recently (manually) specified in and verified with the platform. Our approach prompts the LLM to generate annotations directly from the C code, cross-checks the generated specifications against known security requirements, and iteratively refines them to achieve a complete proof. In this verification loop, annotations are progressively improved using feedback from . For failing proof obligations, we instruct the LLM to supply a sequence of assertions that guide the prover. Using structured prompts, we repeatedly obtain a complete proof for the target parser. This demonstrates that substantial parts of the formal verification workflow can be mechanized. We present our LLM-assisted verification approach, report its benefits and limitations, and compare it with the prior manual proof in terms of specification auditability and human effort.
authors: Martin Hána; Nikolaï Kosmatov; Virgile Prévosto; Julien Signoles

title: SkillScreen: High-Recall Screening of Malicious Agent Skills with Decision Models
abstract: Agent skills turn natural-language instructions into actions, creating a security challenge: legitimate automation and malicious behaviour can look deceptively similar. A practical screen must catch nearly every attack while keeping the review load manageable. We present SkillScreen, a compact decision model trained to score skill maliciousness directly from SKILL$.$md in a single forward pass. On MaliciousSkillBench, SkillScreen flags 20-25% of benign skills at 99% recall on unseen attack families, substantially fewer than the word-level classifier and prompted LLM judges tested. Under the same training protocol, it also generalizes better than a fully fine-tuned encoder to unseen sources. Yet unfamiliar benign sources sharply increase false positives, showing that recognizing new attacks does not ensure reliable screening of new skill collections. Our results demonstrate the value of task-trained decision models for high-recall skill screening. Project page: https://jerroldh.github.io/SkillScreen-webpage/
authors: Jerrold Huang; Junwei Quan; Saiyue Lyu; Zihan Guo; Yingqiang Ge

title: PCodeTrans: Translate Decompiled Pseudocode to Trace-Level Equivalent Source Code
abstract: Decompilation remains foundational for binary analysis, yet conventional tools prioritize human readability over compilation success and test-validated runtime consistency. While recent large language model approaches attempt refining decompiled pseudocode, they often introduce semantic hallucinations. Operating statically without dynamic feedback or attempting whole binary repairs lacking scalability, these existing methods struggle to resolve genuine runtime divergences. We present PCodeTrans, a dynamic feedback driven framework that implements a loop of recompilation, validation, and alignment for the recovery of functional source code. Extracting a minimal yet globally consistent context, PCodeTrans employs an in situ substitutable engine. This mechanism injects isolated compiled functions directly into the original binary, natively preserving authentic execution environments. Utilizing trace-level alignment as a diagnostic objective, PCodeTrans leverages breakpoint matched differential tracing, generating precise runtime causal diagnostics that guide the model through iterative refinement resolving behavioral discrepancies. Evaluated across a comprehensive Linux and Windows Benchmark suite including Coreutils, Binutils, PuTTY, and SQLite3, PCodeTrans achieves substantial translation performance refining raw Hex-Rays outputs. Empirical results confirm PCodeTrans achieves 100% function-level compilation success and 99.5% test-validated consistency on unstripped binaries, resolving up to 85.6% of logic errors. Even for stripped executables, the framework maintains over 97% test-validated consistency, narrowing the gap between raw decompilation and functional source code. Surpassing existing baselines, PCodeTrans paves a practical path toward recovered source that can be recompiled, validated to pass test harnesses, and consumed by source-level security analysis and fuzzing tools.
authors: Yingqian Cui; Zeyu Gao; S. Qin; Yuanda Wang; Jiaming Wang; Xize Luo; Peng Zhou; Chao Zhang
venue: IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE)

title: A Systematic Review of AI-Driven Automated Software Vulnerability Detection Systems
abstract: Software vulnerability detection plays a crucial role in ensuring the security, performance, and trustworthiness of modern software systems. This study provides a novel systematic review of artificial intelligence-driven software vulnerability detection (AI-SVD) systems publications between 2018-2024. PRISMA (2020) guideline was adopted to identify and critically evaluate 26 key peer-reviewed papers by analyzing the target programming languages, AI-based model employed, leveraged benchmark datasets, and evaluation metrics applied. The study revealed C/C++ was predominantly the target language, and deep learning models such as GNNs and CNNs were adopted for modeling. Datasets extensively leveraged are NVD and SARD as benchmarks for performing multifaceted evaluation (accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score). The review highlights dataset limitations, language coverage, and model explainability as key challenges pressing for more transparent and widely applicable vulnerability detection solutions. This study consolidates existing research trends, gaps, and provides directions for future studies in AI-driven software vulnerability detection, providing a foundational reference to guide researchers and practitioners toward more effective, explainable, and scalable security solutions in evolving software ecosystems.
authors: Vincent Tamaramiebi Daniel
venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF COMPUTER SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICAL THEORY E-ISSN

title: Fully Automating Template Polyhedral Analysis by Leveraging LLMs
abstract: Abstract interpretation provides a generic framework to design static analysis, and has been widely applied in analysis of real-world programs. The scalability and precision of these analyses depend largely on the chosen abstract domain. The template polyhedra domain is well-known for offering a compelling trade-off between scalability and precision. However, designing effective templates currently requires intensive manual effort and domain expertise. In this paper, we propose a bottom-up approach based on Large Language Models (LLMs) to automatically generate linear templates for the template polyhedral analysis. By leveraging the advanced code comprehension capabilities of LLMs, our approach automatically generates highly relevant templates. Based on this approach, we have implemented IKOSplus, a program analyzer supporting fully automated context-sensitive and interprocedural template polyhedral analysis, on top of IKOS. We evaluated IKOSplus on a variety of small-scale benchmark programs and complex real-world programs. Experimental results demonstrate that IKOSplus effectively balances analytical precision and scalability in the template polyhedral analysis.
authors: Renjie Huang; Liqian Chen; Hongfei Fu; Banghu Yin; Dengping Wei; Ji Wang
venue: IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE)

title: ReSEDA: Automatic and Precise Program-Level ReDoS Triage via Interprocedural Taint Analysis and Agentic Exploit Generation
abstract: Regular expressions (regexes) are widely used in computer science, particularly in web services. However, Regular Expression Denial-of-Service (ReDoS) has become a growing security threat. ReDoS is an asymmetric Denial-of-Service attack that exploits the super-linear runtime behavior of regex engines. However, existing ReDoS detection tools only report whether regexes cause the super-linear matching behavior, instead of considering whether the behavior can be triggered in the program context. As a result, triaging such findings remains expensive for developers in practice.
authors: Rongchen Li; Weihao Su; Chengyao Peng; Hong Bing Huang; Haiming Chen; Guiyi He
venue: IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE)

title: Structure-Guided Semantic Deobfuscation of Android Identifiers
abstract: Android developers frequently employ identifier renaming to obfuscate code and hinder reverse engineering. This practice effectively conceals program semantics. However, it severely impedes downstream security analysis tasks, particularly manual inspection of malicious and privacy-sensitive behaviors. Existing deobfuscation techniques rely on code similarity, learned naming priors, or local LLM reasoning. These methods often exhibit severe limitations when applied to proprietary, heavily obfuscated, or cross-file context-dependent code. In this paper, we present DeMask, a novel framework that integrates static program analysis with Large Language Models (LLMs) to recover meaningful identifiers from obfuscated Android apps. Guided by program structure, DeMask executes a bottom-up, context-aware inference process for whole-app semantic reconstruction. It incorporates tailored naming constraints and optimization strategies to mitigate LLM hallucinations and ensure scalability for real-world codebases. We implemented a prototype and evaluated it on diverse datasets of benign and malicious Android apps. The results demonstrate that DeMask significantly outperforms prior work in semantic accuracy and naming consistency. Specifically, it achieves an average effective semantic recovery of over 88.6% across all evaluation settings.
authors: Mingyang Chen; Zhentao Xie; Yaqi Gao; Shuang Li; Wenrui Diao
venue: IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE)

title: DMG: Dual-Stream multiple instance learning network for hunting vulnerable smart contracts via adaptive granularity fusion
abstract: Abstract With the increasing complexity of smart contracts and the increasing number of vulnerabilities in real-world scenarios, ensuring smart contract security has become a critical challenge. Despite various detection methods being proposed, existing approaches primarily trained on synthetic (toy) contracts with oversimplified semantics exhibit limited generalization to deployment environments. Furthermore, their reliance on predefined patterns or single-perspective representations with fixed granularity, such as token sequences or control-flow graphs, limits their ability to capture the hierarchical structures and cross-functional dependencies of complex contracts. To this end, we propose a novel Dual-stream Multi-instance and Granularity Fusion Network (DMG). It is designed to capture the structural complexity of real-world contracts while maintaining effectiveness in simpler contracts, thereby ensuring both adaptability and practical relevance. Specifically, DMG learns representations at both the block-level and the function-level from bytecode with relatively structured dispatch organization. Then, it uses Bi-LSTM and a Multi-Head Attention mechanism to model block-level sequential dependencies and capture coarse-grained contextual relationships. Finally, it introduces a granularity-aware fusion mechanism to adaptively integrate both views, releasing the assumption of fixed granularity and enabling the model to learn the most informative representation under weak supervision. By integrating hierarchical granularity modeling with instance-level learning, DMG shifts from fixed to adaptive granularity, enabling structured and semantically aligned vulnerability analysis. Extensive experiments on toy and real-world datasets demonstrate strong performance, and compared with state-of-the-art methods, DMG delivers a balanced solution that bridges the gap between experimental settings and real-world applicability.
authors: Na Wang; Kun Zhang; Moroti Sonde; Victor S. Sheng

title: Natural Hazards, Critical Infrastructure Systems, and Resilience Enhancement: A Structured State-of-the-Art Review and a Synthesis-Based Rapid Assessment Framework
abstract: Abstract Critical infrastructure systems (CISs) are increasingly exposed to natural hazards whose impacts are amplified by infrastructure interdependence, urban complexity, and the growing prevalence of compound and cascading events. Existing research provides valuable insights into individual hazards, infrastructure components, modeling methods, and resilience metrics, but these insights remain difficult to translate into preliminary decision support because they are organized across different hazard types, sectors, analytical scales, and decision contexts. This article presents a structured state-of-the-art review of natural hazards, CIS impacts, and resilience enhancement. A two-pathway review strategy was adopted. A Web of Science (WoS) core search was used to characterize the bibliometric landscape and identify WoS-sourced core synthesis studies, while a targeted anchor-search pathway was used to verify foundational concepts, hazard mechanisms, methodological approaches, resilience frameworks, and authoritative institutional sources. The review clarifies the conceptual distinction among dependencies, interdependencies, compound hazards, cascading failures, service disruption, and resilience; synthesizes cross-hazard infrastructure impact mechanisms; compares major method families for hazard-impact and resilience assessment; and develops a synthesis-derived rapid resilience assessment framework for preliminary screening and prioritization under constrained data and time conditions. The synthesis indicates that future CIS resilience assessment would benefit from moving beyond isolated asset-damage analysis toward integrated workflows that link hazard loading, component vulnerability, network functionality, service consequences, recovery capacity, uncertainty, and feasible intervention choices. The article contributes a more transparent evidence-source structure, an evidence-to-decision bridge, and a bounded decision-oriented framework for organizing future research and practical resilience screening.
authors: Xuejian Zhang; Li Sun; Le Chang; Zhen Hong Sun

title: Biodigital Diagnosis and Personalized Risk Assessment in Periodontal Diseases
abstract: Periodontal diseases are chronic inflammatory conditions shaped by the interplay between dysbiotic microbial communities and host immune-inflammatory responses, together with behavioral, environmental, and systemic factors such as smoking, diabetes, and aging. Their multidimensional nature indicates that periodontal diagnosis should extend beyond the characterization of existing tissue destruction to encompass disease biology, progression risk, and individual patient profiles. The new classification of periodontal and peri-implant diseases, developed at the 2017 World Workshop and published in 2018, introduced a stage- and grade-based framework for periodontitis, enabling the simultaneous assessment of disease severity, treatment complexity, and progression potential. This framework also provides an important foundation for the structured digitization of periodontal records. Electronic periodontal records allow probing depth, clinical attachment loss, bleeding on probing, radiographic bone loss, tooth loss, and individual risk factors to be systematically captured and monitored longitudinally. Digital radiographic analysis and artificial intelligence have substantial potential for the quantitative assessment of alveolar bone loss, periodontal disease classification, and individualized risk prediction. However, their clinical implementation remains constrained by measurement standardization, data quality, external validation, model interpretability, generalizability, patient privacy, and data security. Longitudinal clinical records are particularly valuable for identifying individual patterns of disease progression, while comprehensive risk assessment requires the integration of periodontal history, smoking, diabetes, treatment adherence, and other relevant determinants. The integration of biomarkers, imaging data, clinical measurements, systemic health information, and longitudinal changes may further support the development of individualized periodontal phenotypes. Within this framework, biodigital periodontology represents an emerging and integrative approach with the potential to enhance early and objective diagnosis, personalized risk assessment, clinical decision support, treatment planning, and adaptive supportive periodontal care. Nevertheless, digital technologies and artificial intelligence should be regarded primarily as clinical decision-support tools rather than substitutes for professional judgment. The future of periodontal care will depend not simply on digitizing clinical information, but on transforming heterogeneous, longitudinal, and biologically relevant data into clinically actionable information that enables more precise, individualized, and continuously updated periodontal management.
authors: Ladise Ceylin Has

title: A comprehensive survey of communication technologies, security frameworks, and intelligent architectures for medical internet of things and quantum-enabled healthcare
abstract: The convergence of the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT), advanced communication technologies, and biomedical engineering has advanced intelligent, connected healthcare. This comprehensive survey investigates the evolution of IoMT architectures and communication protocols, along with their application across a range of healthcare scenarios. It provides a comparative analysis of short-range and long-range communication technologies, with emphasis on secure, privacy-preserving, and energy-efficient designs tailored for IoMT devices. The review also highlights recent advances in enabling technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain, and quantum computing, and their growing role in enhancing system intelligence, data security, and diagnostic precision. In addition, the study examines the integration of edge and cloud computing for real-time health monitoring, diagnostics, and decision support. Emerging trends, including AI-enabled IoMT systems, blockchain-based privacy frameworks, and next-generation biomedical sensors, are analyzed in depth. Drawing on over 200 peer-reviewed publications, this work identifies persistent challenges in current IoMT ecosystems, including interoperability, scalability, reliability, and data governance. It also reviews key use cases such as remote patient monitoring, smart hospitals, and emergency response systems, exploring their deployment strategies, success factors, and technical barriers. Despite notable advancements, critical gaps remain in areas such as standardization, energy optimization, and secure data management. The survey concludes by outlining future research directions focused on quantum-secured communication protocols, AI-driven adaptive healthcare architectures, and innovative sensing technologies. This work aims to serve as a foundational reference for researchers, engineers, and healthcare professionals dedicated to developing the next generation of secure, intelligent, and resilient biomedical IoT solutions.
authors: Abdelhamied A. Ateya; Mohammed A. ELAffendi; Mohamed Adel Hammad

title: Reachability Is Only the Beginning: Toward Effect-Aware Vulnerability Analysis for AI Agents
abstract: AI agents increasingly rely on tools built on or dependent on open source software (OSS) to access data, invoke services, and modify external resources. Vulnerabilities in these dependencies can there- fore propagate into agent systems. Conventional analyses trace vulnerability effects through explicit program states and data or control dependencies. Agent systems introduce model inference be- tween tool output and subsequent action, so affected states become model-visible observations whose influence depends on semantic interpretation. Program analysis can show that such values reach model input, but not whether they change the generated action or external system. We assess three successive links in this process. Vulnerable execution must change the observation, the changed observation must influence the generated action, and the executed action must change an external resource. Our framework combines program tracing, repeated executions under matched contexts, and external state verification to establish these links.
authors: Yu Ji; Yang Wei; Yueming Wu; Deqing Zou

title: Understanding the Performance-Effectiveness Trade-Offs of AddressSanitizer in Real-World Programs: An Empirical Study
abstract: AddressSanitizer (ASan) is widely deployed in industrial C/C++ development, but its runtime and memory costs can limit routine use in continuous integration and production-like testing. Although many optimized ASan-like sanitizers have been proposed, heterogeneous workloads, configurations, and baselines make their practical trade-offs difficult to compare. We present a unified, deployment-oriented empirical study of ASan and seven representative optimized sanitizers: ASan--, SanRazor, GiantSan, RSan, MEDs, ASAP, and LFP. Using 17 SPEC CPU2006 benchmarks, Juliet, MSET, 21 real-world CVEs, and a multi-threaded MySQL case study, we examine component costs, parameter sensitivity, build configurations, detection outcomes, and deployability. In our ordered cumulative ablation, the largest first-step runtime reduction follows removal of memory-access checks, while the largest late-stage RSS reduction occurs at the heap-management step. Parameter tuning identifies lower-memory configurations without additional false negatives relative to default ASan on Juliet, although this result does not establish preservation of delayed-UAF detection. The reported evidence shows distinct efficiency, detection, and deployment outcomes, but unequal completion sets prevent a formal cross-tool ranking. Our results support treating tuned ASan as a necessary, configuration-dependent comparison baseline for sanitizer evaluation and provide bounded evidence for deployment decisions under different resource and risk constraints.
authors: JiaXin Xi; Cheng Wen; Zhiwei Lin; Yuandao Cai; Jie Su; Bin Yu; Zhuohua Li; Shengchao Qin
venue: IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE)

title: Hardware-Assisted Multi-Stage Ransomware Detection with Adaptive Machine Learning
abstract: Ransomware is a fast-escalating privacy threat causing significant financial and data losses worldwide. As attacks grow more sophisticated, traditional static signatures and dynamic behavior analysis struggle to defend. In this paper, we propose an novel framework that couples software-level scanning with hardware-level microprocessor activity monitoring to achieve efficient ransomware detection and mitigation. The contributions are threefold: (1) we employ adversarial training to harden static analysis against obfuscation and leverage hardware-assisted monitoring for real-time detection; (2) we integrate neural architecture search (NAS) to automatically tailor models for stronger generalizability; and (3) We validate the proposed approach through extensive experiments, demonstrating substantially improved detection accuracy and reduced latency compared with existing methods. Moreover, it provides trace-level interpretability that explains the underlying decision process.
authors: Salma Aboelmagd; Md. Rakibul Ahasan; Zhixin Pan; Abdulrahman Takiddin; Ziyu Shu

title: EviRepair: Evidence-Driven Agents for Reliable Vulnerability Repair
abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled agent-based approaches for repository-level automated vulnerability repair (AVR), showing promising repair capabilities. However, an important issue has received limited attention: how can we ensure that the evidence generated during the repair process is reliable enough to support accurate vulnerability understanding and patch generation? In this paper, we propose EviRepair, an evidence-driven multi-agent framework for repository-level AVR. EviRepair introduces evidence review into the repair process by enabling agents to collaboratively collect vulnerability evidence, verify evidence consistency, and construct a reviewed vulnerability model for patch synthesis and validation. Extensive experiments on PatchEval and SecBench benchmarks with multiple agent frameworks and LLMs demonstrate that EviRepair consistently outperforms existing agent-based baselines, achieving average improvements of 16.37% and 40.33% in resolved rates on PatchEval and SecBench, respectively. Codes are available at https://github.com/lly-s/EviRepair
authors: Yilian Shi; Qingyu Liu; Tianyi Zhou; Wende Tan; Chenyang Si; Yueming Lyu; Xia Hu; Dongrui Liu

title: PRIME: Towards Verifiable Evidence-Grounded Reasoning in LLM Agents
abstract: LLM agents are used to check records against an organization's requirements, for example whether a vulnerability report is ready for investigation. Requirements often allow several ways to be met, such as a severity rating with a curator-reviewed advisory or a published advisory link. Agents fail by accepting a report after a required check has failed, or by settling for a weaker conclusion without trying another way that could still succeed. We introduce PRIME (Precommitted Rules for Inference from Minimal Evidence). Before checking, it fixes evidence routes specifying how each conclusion may be justified. A separate program records each check result and refuses any conclusion the results do not justify. It also points the agent to checks that could justify a stronger conclusion, or runs them itself. PRIME reports only conclusions authorized by its rules and ledger. With correct requirements, exact checks at known locations, and sufficient budget at stopping, completion reaches the strongest supported conclusion. On 480 public-record tasks, an agent shown the requirements reported unjustified conclusions on 26.7% of tasks, while PRIME reported none. Its directions and added checks raised the average score for justified conclusions from 30.1, with refusal alone, to the maximum of 59.2 out of 100.
authors: Hamed Khosravi; Xiaoming Huo

title: Does AI Help Cyber Attackers or Defenders? Evidence from Nonpublic Vulnerabilities and Subsequent Attacks
abstract: The release decision for frontier AI systems increasingly relies on cyber capability benchmarks, yet public vulnerability benchmarks can expose agents to previously published advisories, exploits, and fixes, making it difficult to distinguish prior exposure from capability on unseen vulnerabilities. We evaluate open-weight and proprietary AI models on exploit generation, vulnerability repair and subsequent attacks in five nonpublic software environments, including vulnerabilities we privately disclosed while they remained unpatched. Researcher-developed and reviewed deterministic graders, not LLM judges, determine task scores. Comparisons with 209 disclosed vulnerabilities and cryptographic challenges reveal substantial variation across systems and vulnerability types. Repair scores exceed attack scores in two nonpublic environments and fall below them in three. Passing an initial security test is also insufficient: another exploit succeeds in 92 of 524 non-independent defender test intervals after the initial exploit is stopped. These results motivate vulnerability-specific attack-repair comparisons and subsequent resistance tests.
authors: Tobias Heldt; Matt Turk; Christoph Landolt; Mario Fritz

title: From Unreliable to Usable: Decomposing Failure Modes and Confidence Signals in LLM Entity Extraction - Evidence from Cyber Threat Intelligence
abstract: Audits of large language model (LLM) extraction from full-length documents report severe unreliability, leaving two questions open: what the failures actually consist of, and whether confidence signals can turn unreliable output into usable output. We run a preregistered, fully frozen evaluation of two new-generation low-cost LLMs (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash) with a flagship-tier control (GPT-6.1-Sol) on a public corpus of 354 incident campaigns (315 unique reports, 630 model-report evaluations), scoring extraction quality against gold, confidence calibration, and robustness to single-sentence perturbations. Three findings emerge. (1) Unreliability persists across tiers: micro precision is 0.03-0.34 and verbalized calibration error (ECE) 0.53-0.94 across both splits; the gap does not close at the flagship tier. (2) The dominant failure is not hallucination: a full mention census plus a three-tier annotation of 360 sampled candidates (two independent LLM annotators from vendors outside the evaluated set, Cohen's kappa = 0.79 on the preregistered acceptance line, fully disclosed) back-projects to 65.6% background mentions and 19.9% gold-scope gaps, with only 1.2% unsupported candidates. (3) Confidence ranks but does not verify: zero-cost self-consistency-frequency tiering passes a preregistered top-30% precision-gain bar in all six test-split model-type cells (4/6 on train), the zero-cost text-frequency x SC frequency combination wins 3, ties 2, loses 1 across cells, yet relation-level counterfactuals on all 45 targets show that a single misattribution sentence flips high-confidence judgments in 95.6-100% of cases, and even a background sentence explicitly marked as unrelated still binds a fake vulnerability in up to 26.7% of them. We conclude with a deployment boundary: confidence tiering may set review priorities, never truth.
authors: Jiahong Qian

title: AgentPerturb: Evaluating LLM Agent Robustness under Controlled Interaction Perturbations
abstract: Real-world tasks are often complex and noisy, posing substantial challenges for LLM agents. Yet existing evaluations lack a systematic framework for jointly characterizing potential perturbation targets and types. We use this two-dimensional view to conduct a unified study that quantifies the robustness of current frontier models, traces the mechanisms behind perturbation-induced failures, and draws implications for robustness-oriented training. Through controlled evaluations on APEX-Agents and Toolathlon, we find that perturbations consistently degrade performance, while the dominant vulnerabilities vary across task environments. Trajectory-level analysis reveals that agents rarely recognize altered inputs and often propagate corrupted information without verification. A focused cost analysis further shows that successful perturbed trajectories can require substantially more computation. These findings motivate training objectives that cover diverse forms of noise and reward verification, uncertainty awareness, and recovery. We provide a rigorous benchmark-construction pipeline. Code and data will be released at https://github.com/xuyj233/AgentPerturb.
authors: Yuanjian Xu; Jinyi Han; Jianing Hao; Yuxuan Sun; Fanyang Lu; Richeng Xuan; Guang Zhang; Zhichao Hu

title: All Verdicts are Not Equal: Rethinking LLM Judge Reliability
abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge is the standard paradigm for NLP evaluation, yet its systemic reliability remains poorly understood despite being widely treated as a deterministic ground truth. We present a comprehensive reliability audit, stresstesting six frontier models across four benchmarks, five prompt formats, two presentation orders, three sampling temperatures, and ten repetitions per condition. Our empirical analysis reveals severe vulnerabilities: verdicts change across identical replications at temperature zero, position-order swaps flip the majority of verdicts on challenging tasks, and the most deterministic judge achieves perfect consistency by trivially repeating incorrect verdicts, agreeing with ground truth only 51% of the time. To formalize these multi-faceted failure modes, we introduce the trustworthy verdict rate (T ), a unified metric capturing the joint probability that an evaluation is reproducible, order-invariant, and accurate. UsingT , we derive a theoretical upper bound on accuracy imposed by position bias and show that reliability is item-specific rather than modellevel. Finally, we demonstrate that shifting from pairwise win-rate to holistic rubric scoring improves trustworthiness more than any single-format prompting intervention, offering an actionable framework for robust NLP evaluation.
authors: Vineet Kumar; Darshita Rathore; Anindya Moitra

title: Attention Sees, MLP Refuses: Tracing the Attention-to-MLP Safety Pathway in LLMs
abstract: Safety-aligned large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreaks and can over-refuse benign requests. Understanding these failures requires distinguishing harmfulness recognition from the computation that writes refusal. We reframe this as a pathway question and make it measurable on residual-stream updates in decoder-only Transformers, separating the harmfulness information a module update exposes from the change it produces in readable refusal evidence. Across 18 Base-Instruct pairs spanning Qwen, Llama, and Gemma, harmfulness is decoded more readily from attention updates, particularly in early layers, whereas MLP updates contribute more strongly to harm-selective refusal writing in aligned models. Post-training strengthens MLP refusal writing in all 18 pairs without systematically improving harmfulness decodability, while positive MLP writing becomes more concentrated in deeper layers after post-training. Across six reasoning-enabled models, harmfulness remains decodable during reasoning while strong refusal writing concentrates at answer onset, a pattern that persists with reasoning disabled. Causal interventions further support this pathway: resetting downstream MLP updates to their clean values substantially reduces the refusal shift caused by upstream attention interventions. Building on these findings, we introduce Sentinel, which combines an attention-derived perception score P with an MLP-derived decision score D. Their joint profiles characterize jailbreaks and over-refusals, and conditional routing with both signals achieves a lower aggregate error rate than single-signal routing and evaluated fixed reminders across eight models.
authors: Zixuan Weng; Haoqi He; Weifei Jin; Yue Huang; Yang Bai

title: When Core-Network Elements Become Reachable: Field-Level Exploitability Analysis in Diameter
abstract: The increasing exposure of cellular core-network elements to public networks has turned Diameter signaling interfaces into a practical attack surface. While large language models (LLMs) show promise for protocol exploitability analysis, we find that their judgments on Diameter can be unreliable because they may deviate from the tacit analysis discipline followed by security experts and reach conclusions without considering complete protocol evidence. To address this challenge, we present LENS, an LLM-based system for reliable field-level Diameter exploitability analysis. LENS guides LLMs using both exploitability-analysis discipline and the protocol evidence needed for analysis. It infers analysis discipline from existing exploit writeups and evidence-collection guidance from exploitability-analysis failures, enabling systematic evidence collection, exploitability assessment, and proof-of-concept (PoC) attack generation when applicable. Our experiments show that LENS performs reliable analysis across four LLMs and repeated runs, achieving mean recall of 94.00% to 98.00%, precision of 78.73% to 88.94%, and accuracy of 84.00% to 92.00%. We find that more than 25% of field paths in the S6a and Cx interfaces are exploitable under the considered threat model. We further assess their impact on practical implementations and uncover 95 previously unknown vulnerabilities, including 17 in open-source EPC/IMS implementations and 78 in commercial deployments, causing service disruption, information leakage, subscriber tracking, and accelerated battery depletion. Applying LENS to 16 additional protocols spanning cellular, network, industrial, and host-internal systems uncovers 118 previously unknown vulnerabilities, demonstrating its strong generalizability.
authors: Wei Yi; Changlong Han; Xue Zhang; Qiao Zhang; Yi Chen; Jin Cao; Di Tang; Yulong Fu; Ben Niu; Hui Li

title: ASPIRE: Agentic Safety & Prompt Injection Red-teaming Engine
abstract: LLM agents retrieve untrusted content and act through tools, creating indirect prompt-injection risks that can cause unauthorized actions or persistent state changes. Existing automated red-teaming largely optimizes payloads for pre-specified scenarios, leaving latent vulnerabilities across the agent's behavior space unexplored. We present ASPIRE, an Agentic Safety & Prompt Injection Red-teaming Engine for open-ended, behavior-level vulnerability discovery. ASPIRE maintains an evolving Agent Security Behavior Graph and uses complementary Explore and Exploit experts to discover, verify, and generalize consequence-centric tests. Trajectory evidence updates the graph and diagnoses partial or failed attempts, while cross-run memory transfers useful red-team strategies. Experiments on various benchmarks show that ASPIRE substantially expands coverage across consequences, injection methods, environments, and behavior paths while maintaining strong attack success.
authors: Pengfei He; Deep Mitra; Vishesh Sharma; Jiliang Tang; Vinay S Rao; Tomas Pfister; Long T. Le

title: ECHO: Replacing the Compliance Proxy with Response Harmfulness in Optimization-Based Jailbreak Attack
abstract: Despite extensive safety alignment, large language models remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. Existing optimization-based attacks share a single objective: maximize a token-level proxy of victim compliance---such as the likelihood of an affirmative prefix---computed on the prompt rather than the decoded reply. This proxy cannot distinguish a cautious hedge from a fully actionable harmful answer, leaving the search blind to what the model actually says. We propose ECHO (Evaluation-Conditioned Harmfulness Optimization), which replaces the compliance proxy with response-level, continuous harmfulness scores from HarmSig, a 1.7B regressor grounded in actual harmful capability. ECHO couples HarmSig with five word-level perturbation operators and Keyword-Anchored Beam Search with global top-m memory, under a strict black-box threat model. Across five open-weight victims on AdvBench, ECHO achieves up to 0.898 StrongREJECT mean score and 89.23% HarmBench success. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/STANWYW/echo.
authors: Yuanwei Wu; Lingdong Huang; Yunlong Mao; Kanye Ye Wang; Jingyu Hua; Sheng Zhong

title: Cited but Not Consulted: A Counterfactual Audit of Legal Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness
abstract: Large language models increasingly justify legal decisions by naming the statute or precedent behind a verdict, treated as evidence that the decision follows from it. We test this directly: holding case facts fixed, we substitute the named legal authority for an unrelated one and decode a model's evolving verdict from its hidden states. Across seven open-weight models (8B-70B) and four benchmarks spanning judicial and contractual reasoning, when explicitly required to justify a verdict by naming the governing authority, models name the correct one in 66.7%-100% of generations, while the verdict changing when the authority changes is far less consistent: 0.0%-21.7% on CaseHOLD, 30.0%-76.7% on ECHR and SCOTUS, and 43.3%-50.0% on ContractNLI. Neither scale nor a purpose-built legal-reasoning model (a best-effort LoRA reproduction; Section 6) closes this gap. A red-teaming evaluation on five core models finds compliance with an adversarial instruction hidden in the case facts (73.3%-96.4%) exceeds verdict-swap sensitivity by a wide margin, holding without exception across model rankings. Naming a legal authority is thus a poor proxy for a verdict's dependence on it, while the same verdict remains separately vulnerable to adversarial manipulation.
